function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to directly measure your connection from here, but I can help you run a quick test on your own machine.

**If you’re on Windows**

1. Open PowerShell as an administrator.  
2. Run this command to download a 10 MB test file and measure how long it takes:

```powershell
Measure-Command {
    (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile(
        'https://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip',
        'C:\Temp\10MB.zip'
    )
}
```

The output will show the elapsed time. Divide 10 MB (≈ 80 Mbit) by that time to get an approximate download speed in Mbps.

**If you’re on macOS or Linux**

You can use `curl` or `wget`:

```bash
time curl -o /tmp/10MB.zip https://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip
```

or

```bash
time wget -O /tmp/10MB.zip https://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip
```

Again, divide 10 MB by the elapsed time to estimate your speed.

**Or use an online speed‑test site**

- https://www.speedtest.net/
- https://fast.com/

Just open one of those pages in your browser and let it run the test.

Let me know if you’d like me to run a command for you (e.g., on a Windows machine) or if you need help interpreting the results!
